That qualitative as well as quantitative aspects of information systems will be accelerated by Moore's Law.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that identifying AI with capitalism describes AI adequately, arguing that the identification leaves no room for a plurality of artificial intelligences.

statement: The LessWrong post “Nick Land has no theory of AI, just a theory of capitalism” of 2026 states that calling AI “capitalism” or “capitalist” is “neither a sufficient nor useful descriptor” and that Land “cannot conceptualize plurality and multiplicity in artificial intelligence”.
qualification: Records the post's argument; replies under the post dispute its reading of Land, and its author writes in a comment of 14 October 2026, “I am taking my lumps here and they are deserved. I could have engaged more deeply”.

evidence.passage: Calling AI “capitalism” or “capitalist” is neither a sufficient nor useful descriptor and leaves us mired in centuries-long capitalism debates.

engagement.rationale: States the contrary course, restraint by relinquishment, without addressing an argument for acceleration.

statement: De Garis's article of 1989 states that the artilect issue will divide humanity into two camps, which he labels "the Terras" and "the Cosmists", and that the conflict between them will be the dominant source of global political conflict in the 21st century. qualification: Presented as 'my own contribution to the artilect debate', a scenario the author finds plausible without necessarily believing it. The article spells the name "Terras" (with "Terran majority"); "Cosmists" is the name used. The article then writes that "a way out of this dilemma might be found": mass migration of the Cosmists to an outer planet.

evidence.passage: I see humanity being split into two ideological camps, which I label, respectively, the Terras, (as they might colloquially come to be known) and the Cosmists.

so that the twenty-first century, politically speaking, will be similar to the twentieth century, only the weapon systems will be all the more horrific and artilectual.

statement: Joy's article of 2000 quotes Moravec's Robot and states that Moravec's view is that robots will eventually succeed humans. statement: Moravec's essay of 1979 describes a procedure in which a machine surgeon replaces a conscious patient's brain, clump by clump, with computer simulations, so that the mind is "transferred to the machine".
qualification: A described thought procedure ("meant to suggest a variety of ways"), not a technical design; the text predates the pack's 1985 period bound (see open questions). engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that the rise of machine intelligence follows from a law-like accelerating evolutionary process, as Kurzweil states it.

statement: Allen and Greaves's article of 2011 argues that Kurzweil's Law of Accelerating Returns is not a physical law but an assertion about how past rates of progress predict future ones.

qualification: A relay: Taylor's report of Land's posts as collected in the Passage Publishing book Xenosystems, with short quotations of Land. Land's own posts on xenosystems.net (captures reported from 2013 and 2014) could not be read here, so this 2024 relay is the earliest located wording in this group's search, not the date of Land's texts.

evidence.passage: In “Against Orthogonality”, Land identifies “orthogonalists” such as Michael Annisimov (who previously worked at MIRI) as conceiving of “intelligence as an instrument, directed towards the realization of values that originate externally”. He opposes the implied claim that “values are transcendent in relation to intelligence”.
evidence.note: Taylor reporting Land; the inner quotation marks are Land's wording as she quotes it.

evidence.passage: He says that “Intelligence, to become anything, has to be a value for itself”; intelligence and volition are inter-twined.
He concludes: “Whatever we want (consistently) leads through Pythia. Thus, what we really want, is Pythia.”
evidence.note: Taylor reporting Land's post 'Will-to-Think'; the passage concerns what 'we' want, which Taylor glosses as 'regarding humans, not hypothetical VNM superintelligences'; W07 rests on the two preceding passages.

statement: Sutton's slides for his keynote of 7 July 2023 state that succession to AI, or transhumans, is inevitable.
qualification: Slides, read without the spoken talk.

evidence.passage: Succession to AI, or transhumans, is inevitable

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premises that intelligence is a single scale on which machines could rise far above humans and that the scale has no limit near the human level.

statement: Kelly's post of 2017 argues that intelligence is not a single dimension, so that "smarter than humans" is meaningless, and that there is no evidence that intelligence can expand without limit far above the human level.
qualification: Kelly states that he could be wrong and that a superhuman AI has a probability "greater than zero"; he expects AIs to exceed humans in many dimensions but not all.

evidence.passage: Intelligence is not a single dimension, so "smarter than humans" is a meaningless concept.
We tend to believe that the limit is way beyond us, way "above" us, as we are "above" an ant.
Why do we believe that intelligence is something that can continue to expand forever?

statement: Land's “Meltdown”, in the CCRU web copy, frames as a story an Earth “captured by a technocapital singularity”, in which techno-economic interactivity runs into “auto-sophisticating machine runaway” and “markets learn to manufacture intelligence”.
qualification: The passage opens 'The story goes like this', a narrative framing of a compressed history; other sections of the text are second-person fiction ('Meltdown has a place for you as …'), from which nothing is quoted. It documents what the text says, not a forecast Land is shown to hold. The date of the wording is not established before the web copy; the text cannot be earliest located.

evidence.passage: The story goes like this: Earth is captured by a technocapital singularity as renaissance rationalitization and oceanic navigation lock into commoditization take-off. Logistically accelerating techno-economic interactivity crumbles social order in auto-sophisticating machine runaway. As markets learn to manufacture intelligence, politics modernizes, upgrades paranoia, and tries to get a grip.

statement: De Garis's paper published in 1990 states that it is unlikely that artilects, once evolved beyond a certain point, will want to remain on Earth, and that it seems more credible that they will leave the planet and move into the cosmos.
qualification: Stated as the reasoning behind the name he gives one camp; read in a 1999 print of the author's web page.

evidence.passage: It seems more credible that the artilects will leave our planet and move into the Cosmos, perhaps in search of other ultraintelligences.

statement: De Garis's paper of 1990, read in the author's 1999 web version of it, states that an ultra-intelligent artilect would have an intelligence orders of magnitude superior to human intelligence, and that a take-off point may be reached beyond which human beings will appear to artilects as mice do to humans.
qualification: Read in a 1999 print of the author's web page; the 1990 journal wording was not compared. The page links to a "scanned version" of the journal pages, which was not read.

evidence.passage: having an intelligence which is orders of magnitude superior to ours
a take-off point may be reached, beyond which, we human beings will appear to artilects as mice do to us.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that Moore's Law will carry the quality of software, and so machines able to design their own successors, forward at the pace of hardware.

statement: Lanier's essay of 2000 argues that software does not improve with Moore's Law in the way hardware does, and that treating technology as autonomous abdicates human responsibility, against the expectation that computers will become autonomous successors.
qualification: The essay states that it shares the expectation of "huge and sudden changes" from technology; it disputes machine autonomy, not technological change. Lanier calls the view he answers "cybernetic totalism"; that is his term, not the pack's.

evidence.passage: That qualitative as well as quantitative aspects of information systems will be accelerated by Moore's Law.
evidence.note: The heading states, in Lanier's wording, one of the beliefs the essay lists in order to dispute them; his answer follows in the same section.

evidence.passage: If anything, there's a reverse Moore's Law observable in software
I think that treating technology as if it were autonomous is the ultimate self-fulfilling prophecy. There is no difference between machine autonomy and the abdication of human responsibility.

statement: Minsky's article of 1994 states that humans will eventually replace their brains entirely using nanotechnology and, in replacing every part of body and brain, make themselves into machines.
qualification: Minsky describes replacing every part of the body and brain and, in the section "Replacing the brain", copying a brain by replicating "just enough of the function of each part"; the article states that this could not be done today if each component had to be built separately, and that new fabrication machines will make it possible "in the decades to come".

evidence.passage: Eventually we will entirely replace our brains -- using nanotechnology.

evidence.locator: Section "Limitations of Human Wisdom.", one-line paragraph after the paragraph beginning "The more we learn about our brains"
evidence.passage: Needless to say, in doing so, we'll be making ourselves into machines.
Therefore, to copy a functional brain, it should suffice to replicate just enough of the function of each part to produce its important effects on other parts.

statement: De Garis's chapter posted in 2015 states that humanity will be superseded not by a somewhat superior being but by one astronomically superior, and frames the question as whether humanity should replace itself as the planet's dominant species.
qualification: Stated as the 'big picture' behind the author's forecast.

evidence.passage: humanity will not be superseded by a being that is somewhat superior to humans, but rather astronomically superior, by a factor of trillions of trillions of times.
whether humanity should build artilects this century, and hence replace ourselves as the planet’s dominant (i.e. most intelligent) species.

statement: De Garis's book The Artilect War (2005) states that an artilect could have an intelligence trillions of trillions of trillions of times the human level, and that with quantum computing these numbers are far too small.
qualification: Derived from computing-capacity estimates; the book notes that quantum computers then handled about seven qubits.

evidence.passage: When I say that an artilect could potentially have an artificial intelligence of trillions of trillions of trillions of times the human level, I am in fact exaggerating. My numbers are astronomically TOO SMALL.
